label: paragraph_title
text: A-WELCOME PHASE.

label: text
text: Purely local affairs have receded in the background during the last few weeks, owing to the situation in Shanghai and Canton occupying the public mind to the exclusion of anything else. It is certainly a change from the "daily armed robbery" that was a feature of the daily papers not so long ago, although this form of crime is by no means conspicuous by its absence. That there would be fewer armed robberies if the Police were given the support of the Chinese community to a greater extent goes without saying.

label: text
text: Time and again the special difficulties of the Police have been commanted upon—difficulties that are rendered greater by the utter lack of co-operation even amongst the victims of this phase of crime. Too often has the case against a suspect been brought almost but not quite—to the point of conviction only to break down on the question of identity. These most disastrous—the

label: text
text:
turn their heads so that they could not see the faces of the criminals, or at least swear that they did so, with the result that too often have thorough despera- does had to be discharged owing to the lack of sufficient evidence of identity. There has been no community spirit — no zeal in helping the Police based on a willingness to help the community generally to rid itself of undesirables whose only vocation is that of armed robbery. There was a welcome phase, however, at yesterday's Criminal Sessions, this being the disclosure during the hearing of three cases of armed robbery that arrests were made possible either through Chinese women giving the alarm or being able to identify the prisoners subsequently. Furthermore, in one case in Shanghai Street, a woman was bound and gagged, but somehow got free and was plucky enough to give chase to one of her assailants whom she asked a man in the street to catch, which he declined to. Eventually, at the invitation of the Police he found and identified the prisoner, who was sentenced to five years' imprisonment. Had this woman followed the too prevalent practice of "turning her head away" until the robbers had made a clean "get away," at least one of her assailants would not now have five years in which to repent of his misdeeds—or at least to regret the pluck of the woman that led to his capture and conviction.
There may be no “medals for valour” in cases of this kind, but there certainly should be some recognition, however slight, of the bravery of the woman who actually gave chase to a man armed with a dagger who had assisted to gag and bind her and rob her house. Failing something being done in this direction it may be worth while ensuring that a report of the three cases at the Criminal Sessions mentioned is published in the vernacular papers by way of encouraging other Chinese women to exhibit a spirit of pluck and community interest. It is a trait all too rare, and when it is discovered it should be fostered. Even a personal word of commendation from the Captain Superintendent of Police or the Secretary of Chinese Affairs might have an excellent moral effect.

The game of "If" is one that we suggest even the most sarpedicized.
exempt in from reason's rule. The other day the papers recorded two stories of voluntary poverty which must have provoked in their readers a perfect orgy of the game. One was of a man who, possessed of enormous wealth, preferred to go on living a life of hard work and physical austerity; the other told of a woman who died of starvation with a hoard of money in the house. In several millions of minds the fascinating "If" must have risen, to mock and tantalise. If we had had those millions, we should not have continued to prefer our feet as a means of progression, to a motor-car. If we had needed food, we should most certainly have preferred it to a bag of money. These "ifs" are entirely useless: moralists and psychologists unite in telling us that they are even actually pernicious, because they distract our attention from the real world to the false, weaken the will-power, and in general lead to slackness and decay. But we go on indulging them: In extreme cases, perhaps, the indictment is true. There are people who live so entirely in dreams that they constitute a perpetual burden and irritation to their families and friends. They might murmur, in the words of the poet:

label: text

Is like a pleasant sleep,
Wherein I rest, and heed

label: text
text: The dreams that by me sweep.—but that they—or at least some of them—let duties and responsibilities sweep by them unheeded, and only wake up now and then, with a start to borrow a dollar or so. But, kept in bounds, the game of if is harmless enough. It certainly gives pleasure.

label: paragraph_title
text: The Average Man.

label: text
text: Is there such a person? An American writer is impressed with the persistent thought that the biggest force in the States today is the average man. If this applies to America, it must surely apply to other places. It may be argued by precise persons, he says, that the average man does not exist that each individual develops traits which either bring him over, or under, the average. But, he goes on, it is true that the average man is true to type. He becomes a representative of the nation. He lives in the average way; eats, drinks, and works in the average manner; makes an average living and when he dies has an average funeral and the average obituary notice of average brevity. He is the strength of the community, the contented man, the happy man. He does not crave for notoriety; he is fairly well satisfied with the conditions that govern his life. His ambition is tempered with caution: He steers a middle course between the Charybdis of baffled aspirations and the Scylla of despair....The picture is not at all convincing. It is like the curate's egg—good in parts. If it were wholly true we would pray for mercy for the world. It is true that the globe is peopled in part with this easy-going type of person; but it is equally true to say that the world's progress—its advance in all the arts and sciences—is due to those whom it would be an affront to describe as the average man. The seeker after truth and after knowledge is far from average. For which let us give thanks.

label: text
text: Our police are to go into shorts and puttles in the rainy

label: text
text: the rainy weather and there will be a consequently heavier tax on the resources of the police store-house in respect of khaki material. Few know of this building's existence but it is situated at the western end of the police compound and within are transacted daily incidents which would bring a reminiscent smile to the face of any ex-service man who happened to pass when the door was open. What tales the police equivalent of the army quartermaster there must have to listen to and what a Solomon he must be to discriminate rightly as to the merits of the excuses offered for the free replacement of missing articles! For instance, if Sergt. Blank can get a topee replaced without inconvenient deductions from his pay because it was "blown from his head on a bathing picnic," is the same procedure to apply in the case of Constable? who maintains that his was lost in the pursuit of duty in the shape of a fleeing malefactor? The question is asked in all innocence and ignorance and probably there are clearly enough defined rules applying to most cases—as for the rest, if the officer in charge resembles to any great extent the army quartermaster of yore he will be eminently capable of gauging to a nicety the exact proportion of truth and fiction. As regards the actual cost to the force of the articles in question, every precaution is taken to ensure the utmost economy. A glance inside will reveal shelf after shelf of rolls of cloths of all the requisite shades and qualities, and lengths of which are given to the local contractor according to the equipment required. He is even given the buttons and other incidentaries, being merely responsible for labour involved in making up. label: text
text: George Bernard Shaw has contributed a letter to "The Times" on the subject of smallpox and vaccination. This is a subject which is much to the fore at present, there being outbreaks of alleged smallpox in various parts of the country and several fatalities having occurred, both among children and adults following their vaccination.

MUCH WORSH THAN SMALLPOX.
“The resultant slight illnesses” included some that were much worse than any ordinary case of smallpox. The medical report was never published. I have two reasons for inflicting these commonplaces of a vaccination controversy once more on your readers. The first is that the press and the administrative departments seem to be relapsing into that infatuated ignorance of the strength of popular and scientific opposition to vaccination, which received such a shock when the compulsory clauses had been repealed by a scared House of Commons in 1898. If the departments and press persist in ignoring and suppressing the case against vaccination until there is another exclusion, the result may possibly be that vaccination will be made a crime as inoculation (equally well-accredited) has been.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: "My second reason is that although smallpox is now a comparatively negligible disease—so much so that in the little outbreaks which seem so tumpery to those of us who remember 1871 and 1881. We sometimes find no deaths and the whole affair is dismissed by the old hands as chickenpox—yet the shortage of houses has produced so much overcrowding that there is a serious danger that nature may strike again and strike hard as she does always when she is too long" defied.

label: text
text: It is an established fact that more adequate housing sanitation can avert the blow. It is equally an established fact that revaccination cannot. Anything that leads us to rely on vaccination and neglect housing sanitation is therefore most misachievously inopportune at the present time. But for these conditions nothing would have induced me to take up my pen against in an argument with a profession which has surrendered itself to a fixed idea.
